title: Why do objects fall at the same rate in a vacuum?
central_question: If a heavier object is pulled harder by gravity, why does it not fall faster when there is no air?
principle_statement: Where air resistance is negligible, all objects released together at the same place fall with the same acceleration, regardless of their mass.
domain_of_validity: Small objects near a much larger body, negligible air resistance, no other significant forces.

scientific_explanation.level_1: A heavier object is pulled harder by gravity, but it is also harder to get moving. These two effects cancel exactly. On Earth, air pushes back much more on a feather than on a hammer, which is why the feather falls slowly. Take the air away and they fall together.
scientific_explanation.level_2: Near a planet, the acceleration caused by gravity depends on the planet's mass and the distance from its centre. It does not depend on the mass of the falling object. Air resistance is a separate force that depends on shape and speed, so it affects a feather far more than a hammer.
scientific_explanation.level_3: Newton's law of gravitation gives F = G M m / r^2 and Newton's second law gives F = m a. Combining them gives a = G M / r^2, in which the falling object's mass m cancels. This assumes the inertial mass in F = m a equals the gravitational mass in the law of gravitation, an equality that is tested experimentally (the equivalence principle).

supporting_evidence: Apollo 15 (1971): Commander David Scott dropped a geologic hammer and a feather together on the Moon, where there is almost no air, as a live television demonstration.
NASA describes the Moon as a good place, free of air resistance, to test whether objects fall equivalently.

claims.text: At the end of the last Apollo 15 moonwalk, Commander David Scott dropped a geologic hammer and a feather at the same time as a live demonstration for the television cameras.
The Moon is a good place, free of air resistance, to test whether objects of different composition fall equivalently.
Under Newtonian gravity, the acceleration of a small object near a large body is a = G M / r^2, independent of the small object's mass.
The recommended value of the Newtonian constant of gravitation is about 6.674 x 10^-11 m^3 kg^-1 s^-2, with a small stated uncertainty.

dimension_check.rhs: m^3 kg^-1 s^-2 kg kg m^-2

numeric_checks.note: Illustrative: Earth mass and radius here are rounded textbook values with no source recorded. Used only as a sanity check.

assumptions: Air resistance and other forces are negligible.
The falling object is small compared with the attracting body, so the body's own motion can be ignored.
Gravity is treated as uniform over the height of the drop.
Inertial mass and gravitational mass are equal (tested experimentally, assumed in the derivation).

variables.name: distance from the centre of the large body

practical_applications: Predicting the fall of objects and spacecraft trajectories.
Understanding why parachutes and streamlining matter.

misconceptions.correction: Without air resistance they fall together. In air, drag changes the result, and mass is only part of that story.

misconceptions.statement: There is no gravity on the Moon, so things float.
misconceptions.correction: The Moon has gravity, weaker than Earth's. The feather fell because the Moon has almost no air.

misconceptions.statement: The Apollo 15 drop proved the law for all objects.
misconceptions.correction: It was one demonstration. It supports the principle, and precision tests are done in dedicated experiments.

what_if_scenarios.title: What if we ignore air resistance when predicting a drop on Earth?
what_if_scenarios.summary: Predicting that a feather and a hammer land together in air is wrong.
what_if_scenarios.correct: Treat air resistance as a separate force. In air, a feather is slowed far more than a hammer.
what_if_scenarios.overlooked: Assuming air does not matter and predicting that a feather and a hammer land together on Earth.
what_if_scenarios.what_changes: The prediction leaves out the drag force, which depends on shape and speed rather than only on mass.
what_if_scenarios.consequences: The prediction is wrong in air: the hammer lands first.
what_if_scenarios.why: Gravity gives both objects the same acceleration, but drag is a second force that affects the feather far more.
what_if_scenarios.prevention: State the assumption that air resistance is negligible, and check that it holds before using the model.

what_if_scenarios.title: What if we assume mass changes the acceleration?
what_if_scenarios.summary: A mass-dependent model would contradict the Moon drop.
what_if_scenarios.correct: Use a = G M / r^2, in which the falling object's mass cancels.
what_if_scenarios.overlooked: Assuming that a heavier object has a larger acceleration.
what_if_scenarios.what_changes: A mass-dependent model would predict different fall times for a hammer and a feather.
what_if_scenarios.consequences: It would contradict the Apollo 15 demonstration, where the hammer and feather were seen landing together.
what_if_scenarios.why: The larger pull on a heavier object is cancelled by its larger inertia, so the acceleration is the same.
what_if_scenarios.prevention: Check a model against observations such as the Apollo 15 demonstration, and keep the unit and assumption checks.

safety_considerations: Low risk when shown as animation. Do not encourage dropping heavy objects from heights or entering vacuum chambers without supervision.
